utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Mr. Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is the case IT-03-69-T, the Prosecutor versus Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. And before I give an opportunity, because you wanted to address the Chamber, I have two short matters which I'd like to address first, but for the first one we have to move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. On the 23rd of February, the Chamber has granted the Prosecution a three-week extension to respond to the Stanisic Defence's consolidated bar table motion, Mr. Groome. And there was a separate motion concerning three documents only, filed on that same day, the 23rd of February. Now, no response has been received to that motion, and the Chamber understood the Prosecution's arguments for an extension to hold true only for the consolidated motion. But there may have been a misunderstanding. But I would like to inquire whether the Prosecution wanted to respond to the bar table motion of three documents only, because that was filed on the 23rd of February, which means that the time-limits expires this Thursday, I think, on the 8th of the March.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I ask Ms. Marcus to deal with that. She is more familiar with the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Thank you. We did -- it was probably my error, we did take that to be part of the bar table just having been filed separately, so we did make the obviously incorrect assumption that that would all be extended with the deadline. We can certainly respond on those three documents in time for Thursday if Your Honours would prefer. It's possible, though, that the arguments that we might make in that submission would relate to the arguments that we would make in the later submission and we may then just cross-reference it, if that's acceptable to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And -- any preference by the Stanisic Defence? I can imagine to making cross-references is another source of mistakes, isn't it, and it's about three documents only, and that's on the totalities of a limited number. So I wonder whether we should insist on receiving a response on the three by Thursday or that we just include them in the whole bunch.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: In many ways, it makes sense to include them all in the whole bunch, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The extension of time is granted also for the motion relating only to the three documents. Then could the witness be brought into the courtroom. Mr. Petrovic, it will be you who is --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When I read the summary of the anticipated testimony, the -- there are a few lines which sound very familiar to me, Mr. Petrovic, like the witness is expected to testify on the deterioration of interethnic relations in the Republic of Croatia after the first multi-party elections. I have a vague recollection that I've seen this language before, and I also remember that it was sometimes not disputed by the Prosecution that the interethnic relations became worse. Similar, could you please keep in mind very carefully that we are not hearing repetitious evidence, because, especially if it's not the core issues of this case, then I think there would be no need to hear that. There's no great dispute about worsening of the interethnic relations, Ms. Marcus, is there?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Will you also carefully check whether there is anything in the adjudicated facts which might cover any of the topics.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we will do so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Djukic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration. The text is now handed out to you. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Djukic, please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Djukic, the Chamber has been informed about your medical condition. If at any time you would need a break, don't hesitate to address me. We usually take a break after one hour and 15 minutes. A break will then be half an hour. And then we have two more sessions of 75 minutes. Again, divided by a break of half an hour, so that you know, more or less what to expect. But if you need any additional break, don't hesitate to ask for it. You will first be examined by Mr. Petrovic, and Mr. Petrovic is counsel for Mr. Simatovic. Mr. Petrovic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Djukic.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: My name is Petar Djukic, nicknamed Pero. Paragraf.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you give us your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: On the 11th of July, 1942, in Cerik Brcko, Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us where you've completed your primary and secondary education?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: I completed my primary school in the village of Bosanska Bijela in the municipality of Brcko, and I then proceeded to the faculty which I graduated from in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And which university was that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: It was the study of legal affairs, affairs of state administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can we just please make sure that we make a break between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I will need to adapt to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you said that you obtained university degree in Zagreb. Where was that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: First, I attended a two-year course in administration affairs, and then proceeded to study at the law school in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you attend any master courses?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, with the renowned professor, Franjo Bacic. I attended the masters course in criminal law. After I had to leave Zagreb, I applied to defend my masters thesis in Novi Sad. Unfortunately, my duties prevented me from doing so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Sir, where did you first get employment?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: I first got employment as policeman in the village called Drenovci, after I completed the policing school where I was the best in my class.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Sir, did you work for a while in Zupanja and, if so, when was that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: Let me clarify this. Drenovci and Zupanja come under the same secretariat. Drenovci are in a substation. Between 1968 and 1972 I was there, and in Zupanja, charged with crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: It says here that you worked there until 1972. Until which year did you work in Zupanja?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: Until 1972 I was charged with crime. And between 1972 and 1977 I was the commander of the police station in Zupanja.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you were transferred to the Republican Secretariat of the interior in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Let me just say that after the post of the commander of police, I was a police officer charged with defence and management of emergency situations. And then I was transferred to the Republican Secretariat of the interior in the sector for operative affairs, and I was occupying the post of inspector for the method of work --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch what year that was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you repeat the year you are talking about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1982.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, sir, did you at some point defend a dissertation which granted you the highest post in the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. In 1987, I defended the dissertation on the topic of the basic policing duties in the service of public security. Before that, I was appointed to the post of the chief of the police of the Socialist Republic of Croatia, and I had roughly 11.000 subordinates.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, up until here were you employed in the RSUP Croatia?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: Until the 20th of June 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, we will skip the war period for now and I'll ask you to tell us if at the end of 1995 you were received any sort of duty from the international community.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: In the month of December, after the signing of the Erdut Agreement on the peaceful reintegration of the district of Eastern Slavonia, Baranja, and Srem based on which Resolution 1037 was adopted by the Security Council of the United Nations, on the order of certain international representatives, I was charged with running the work of interim police forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djukic, were you appointed to some duty on 1st July 1996 and if so by whom?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: After the UNTAES mission was set up, Ambassador Jacques-Paul Klein appointed me to the post of the chief or head of the interim police forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, it was announced that some documents would be used with this witness. I really wondered whether there was a dispute about an appointment the 1st of July by Mr. Klein of this witness to a certain task. We even received copies of the documents confirming that. I do not know what the exact relevance for this is apart from that apparently that the international community entrusted some tasks to -- to this witness. Have you discussed with Ms. Marcus whether there is any dispute about appointment, task, and, of course, the next steps will be whether they were happy with what the witness did. Certificates of appreciation. Is there any dispute about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't believe that there is any dispute about that, but I want Their Honours to see it. I want this to be heard, because I would like to pin-point the serious affairs that the witness was charged with. It will only take a couple of minutes, and these are the reasons why I would like to present these issues to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Why don't you agree on that with the Prosecution? Why do we have to -- I mean, you have seen that important tasks, we received announcement of these documents to be used, so what you want to pin-point at is -- is first something you could have agreed on because this is no dispute about it. Second, you could have -- you could have sought admission through a bar table exercise because it's perfectly clear what these documents say. So if there is anything in addition to that which sheds a different light on it, please proceed. Otherwise, choose one of these avenues to bring it to our attention. You may have noticed that it is already to our attention, by the way, but not yet as evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in that case, if my colleague doesn't object can 2D1211, 2D1212, and 2D1210 be admitted as Defence exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no objection to 2D1210, or 2D1212. The 2D1211 is a bit of a curious document. We don't contest the facts as Your Honours has set forth that the witness held this position. But the document is just a bit curious. It's unsigned. The original is in B/C/S rather than in English, so I'm just -- I'm curious about that particular document. But we do not contest the facts as asserted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please tell us whether we would receive a translation soon from the document which is apparently -- let me just have a look. The unsigned ones seems to be as 462 --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1211, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's 1211. Ms. Marcus, the copies we received is with handwriting on the top, 462/96 handwritten. That is the unsigned document. We have translation but no signature. Is that --

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- the one you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And it -- if that's -- I'm not sure which one is the original, but assuming it was Jacques Klein who wrote it and it was a UN document, I would think the original is English and the English that I have is a translation of the B/C/S. Neither of them are signed, Your Honour, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I can assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When he came to The Hague, the witness brought along the Serbian version of the document that he received, as far as I understand, at the time when Jacques Klein gave it to him. The Serbian version is the basic one that we use. The translation is one that we've produced, and I think that the witness can help us. He does have the English version of the document which he hasn't brought along The Hague. But if this is contested and if asked, I'm sure that he will find ways to deliver it to us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It is it quite possible for me to bring that over.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have a -- any signed copy of the letter of the 2nd of June in which reference is made to the appointment on the 1st of July?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have the English version back at home. The head of the interim administration was an authority to me. I can't go into how his documents were produced. They never bore a stamp or a seal of any sort, his documents. There was just this designation of the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The English copy you have got at home. Is that a signed letter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I presume so. I can tell you that I received numerous --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- citations in writing from Mr. Klein commending me, and believe me when I tell you it's been a long time ago, so I can't remember all the details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You've answered my question, that you presume that the document at home is signed. Let me just check. 2D1210 and 2D1212 are admitted into evidence and the numbers assigned to these documents, Mr. Registrar, would be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 65 ter document 2D1212 shall be assigned Exhibit D759. And 65 ter document 2D1210 shall be assigned Exhibit D760. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And they're admitted into evidence under these numbers. Then for 2D1211, Mr. Registrar, which will be marked for identification, what number would be assigned?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D761. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Petrovic, to the extent the witness has a signed version of that letter available, we'll invite him to -- to provide us -- Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. We will follow your instructions, as far as this document is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Now, Witness, sir, I just have one question with regard to your relationship with Mr. Klein. Did Mr. Klein ever offer you a job after the completion of your mission in Eastern Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: Well, since it is being questioned here whether I ever was in actual fact the head of the interim police or not, let me just say a few words --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you there. That is not in dispute. It's not challenged. So, therefore, you don't have to worry about that. Did Mr. Klein ever offer you a job, as Mr. Petrovic asked you? A yes or a no simply would do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, he certainly did. And I have to stress that he commended me especially for my great contribution, as did his -- as did Ambassador Walker in January 1998 in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Petrovic, to the extent it was your point to establish that the witness was held in high esteem by -- by Mr. Klein and by others, then that point is clear. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djukic, you said a moment ago that up until 1990, you were employed with the Republic of Croatia SUP. Would you please tell us briefly why you stopped working in the Croatian SUP in June 1990.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: In the Socialist Federal Republic of Croatia after the democratic elections there were fundamental changes in the political order in the state, and I had given my oath to the socialist republic and I was not prepared to defend the political system of any other order.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djukic. Could you please tell us where you went from Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: I want back to Cerik, my birth place, in Brcko municipality because that was the only way out for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djukic, when you arrived in Cerik did you offer your services to any structure or any organisation in that area?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: Since I was 48 years old I was a conscript, according to the Law on The Military Forces, so I reported immediately to the JNA and to the chief of security and intelligence, Mr. Momcilo Petrovic, and I said that I was prepared to offer my services, that I was at his disposal, all in the hope that we would remain within Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, sir, the record does not show which garrison you mentioned so would you please repeat it.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: This was the Brcko garrison. The garrison commander was Colonel Pavle Milinkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Djukic, you said that you worked with the chief of intelligence, Mr. Petrovic. Could you please tell us what that consisted in, how did you work with him, with Mr. Petrovic, and did you have a code-name at the time?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: As I was still in -- officially I was still assigned to Zagreb and I had not received my papers, my code-name was Magistar, Magistar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, sir, did you work with any other officer -- JNA officer at the time? And if we need to move to private session so that you can tell us his name, would you please just let us know?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: Well, I would appreciate it if we could move to private session for benefit of the person in question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objections against going into private session. Although ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The captain who was my connection --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djukic, on instructions from the JNA, did you join any political party at the time and, if so, which one?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: Well, in the area where I lived, there were 19.7 per cent of Serbs. The ratio in the event of war would be 1 to 5. I was asked to join, which was in accordance with the Communist party, I joined the late Professor Nijaz Durakovic's party in Brcko, the social democrats.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djukic, for your answers, but would you please just speak a little more slowly so that all that you say can be reflected in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could you make a pause between question and answer and answer and question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djukic, in Pelagicevo in October 1991, did there come a time when an armed unit arrived there?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. The 17th Tactical Group arrived, headed by Colonel Stevan Nikolic [Realtime transcript read in error "Niklovic"], aka Kriger.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us where the 17th Tactical Group came from?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: It came from Derventa because it was under pressure there from Croatian paramilitary formations, and they tried to avoid young soldiers being killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness could you please repeat the name of the commander of this 17th Tactical Group because it is not correctly recorded in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: Stevan Nikolic, a colonel. His nickname was Kriger because he had a cap that was reminiscent of the cap that was worn by a character from a Belgrade TV series, Otpisani, who was called Kriger.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djukic. Tell us, please, in the autumn of 1991 and in early 1992, did you know what the intentions of the Croatian side were, both the Croatians in the Republic of Croatia as well as in Bosnia and Herzegovina, as far as some areas in the Sava river valley were concerned?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do know of that because I worked for many years in Zupanja and it bordered on the Sava with Bosnia along a stretch of 108 kilometres. The plan of the Croatian forces was to take control of Modrica, Odzak, Samac, Orasje, Brcko, and to cut the corridors so that Knin would remain in the rear supported and that -- that, in fact, so that logistical support could be provided from Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, perhaps because of the speed of your speech not all of the towns that you mentioned were recorded in the transcript. Could you please repeat them? Repeat the towns that you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: Derventa, Modrica, Odzak, Bosanski Samac, Orasje, Brcko; in other words, the Bosnian Posavina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djukic. Could you tell us how the 17th Tactical Group was reinforced militarily, if you know. And I'm referring to this period, late 1991/early 1992.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm very familiar with that. It was reinforced by conscripts in the early days by the very young ones who had just served in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us which towns those conscripts came from and, if you knew, what ethnicity they were?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: They were from all the Serb villages in Gradacac and Samac municipalities, except in Spijunica and Srnice that were separate. And my village Srnice, which had been surrounded by Bukvik --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And interpreter could not catch the other name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- because they did not have any links with the garrison, but the most prominent villages were Batkusa, Slatina, Krusko Polje, and a series of other villages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you -- you really have to slow down because otherwise the interpreters are unable to follow what you say. Could I first seek clarification of the following: Your -- part of your last answer: "... was they were from all the Serb villages in," and what did you then say? "In ... and Samac." What did you first mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Spijunica, Srnice, Cerik, Plazevac, Porebrice, Pelagicevo, Donji Zabar, Obudovac, Slatina, Batkusa, Krusko Polje, and the town Bosanski Samac itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it that what is now still missing will be corrected after having heard the audio. Mr. Petrovic, could you please take care that the witness slows down and that breaks are made. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, both, on behalf of the witness and in my own name, I will say that we will do our best to comply with your instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, sir, you have just told us what villages the reservists who reinforced the 17th Tactical Group were from. Now could you tell us how these individuals were armed and by whom?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: In the first -- at the first stage, the conscripts were armed only in the border areas that had contact with Croatian and Muslim villages because it was assessed that possible attack would come from there. The arming was done exclusively by the JNA and the weapons used for -- for arming them was the -- were the weapons that were envisaged per establishment within the JNA. Per each ten soldiers there would be one machine-gun, six automatic and three semi-automatic rifles, plus handheld launchers; two hand grenades; bayonets, and so on. If necessary, I can add whatever is necessary.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: If there is any -- if anything else was necessary, then it would be added on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djukic. Tell us, please, as these reservists, as you told us, were from the villages in the area of Bosanska Posavina, did they go home when -- from those units? Did they go on home on leave from those units and did they take something with them?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, some of those reservists - and I have to stress this - did take these weapons to their homes, and in the first phase only night patrols were established within villages. They started doing that. And they were -- they were trying to be as discreet as possible so that they would not upset or, rather, bring some restlessness among the other -- the non-Serb population. Although most of them -- most of the population was Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, the reservists who went home on leave, did they organise themselves once they got back to their villages?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: Well, I will repeat again, this was the case only in the border areas of the 17th Tactical Group area of responsibility. Only small units were established; in other words, platoons of up to 30 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who commanded these platoons that were being established within these villages?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: They were under the command of reserve commissioned and non-commissioned officers of the JNA, ones that would normally reside in their homes until they were activated, although not yet mobilised.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djukic, you mentioned the weapons that the reservists had. Can you tell us what was the weaponry at the disposal of the 17th Tactical Group, if you know, in the period we are discussing, end of 1991 and early 1992?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: Of course I know. The 17th Tactical Group had Howitzers of 155 millimetres, tanks T-34, the Pragas, armoured combat vehicles and a number of mortars, 82 and 60 millimetres. In addition to that they had anti-tank assets, Zoljas and Osas, hand-held rocket-launchers.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, sir, do you know within which larger organism was the 17th Tactical Group?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: Until the month of May, they were under the Tuzla Corps under the command of Sava Ivanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter isn't sure about the last name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you repeat the name of the commander. Sava, and then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Jankovic. I apologise. I have a bit of a sore throat.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djukic, you can help yourself to some water. Mr. Djukic, did there come a time when you came in touch with Colonel Nikolic, the commander of the 17th Tactical Group?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. From the day he assumed his position, I was at his disposal at all times. I help him to familiarise himself with the area, the population, the demographics, and the other basic information. For instance, the experience that the local population brought over from the previous war which was that they would not agree to leaving their local areas to fight elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you make any assessments for him, for Mr. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I worked with his officers. I cannot say their worked or produced anything for them, other than providing them with information.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djukic, do you know if, during the fighting in the Republic of Croatia, there was a plane that was shot down somewhere in the area of Samac?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: In Slavonski Brod, which is on the other bank of the Sava river across from Bosanski Samac, a plane was shot down. The pilot ejected himself and the plane crashed in a village there in Croatia. The pilot was saved and with the assistance of the former members of the State Security Service, Simo Zaric, they went to the command of the air force in Belgrade. They brought the pilot back. And as a reward, the peasant who was there and saved the pilot was given a uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that Simo Zaric was a member of the State Security Service. Can you tell us which service was that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: The State Security Service of Bosnia-Herzegovina. He was the head of the forward outpost of that service in Modrica.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You told us that Simo Zaric interceded in this affair where the pilot was taken back to the command of the air force in Belgrade. Did Zaric come into contact with anyone on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know about that. For a great many years I was in contact with Zaric both privately and professionally. He got to know certain generals and commanders who were members of the air force.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: If you can recall, can you give us any names of the generals that Simo Zaric got in touch with?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: It was Bajic, who was the -- the right wing of the partisan football club.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djukic, is that the way you remember that last name or was it a footballer, really?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: Well, I remembered him by the family name of Bajic because I knew a footballer and I was a passionate supporter myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Can you tell us what happened on the 16th of January, 1992; if you know?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: On the 16th of January, 1992, mobilisation was conducted, although it was not part of a general call for mobilisation. I know that - I insisted myself, I had two sons, although they were still minors - that conscripts should have a stamp placed in their military booklets because that would mean that they were in a war and be entitled to certain rights arising from their participation in the war. I was aware of that because I had to deal with some very complex situations while I was one of -- of the leaders of the police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, therefore, what was it that was entered into the military records of all the conscripts in Bosnian Posavina on that particular date?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: Well, there was just a seal and a date affixed to one of the columns there. There was still not a war going on there. The war in Posavina broke out at a later date.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djukic, was it about this time that larger units were being formed in the area of the 17th Tactical Group; if you know?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Military detachments were being formed, and they were strictly units of the JNA. Battalions -- or, rather, detachments were formed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how many of these detachments were there?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: If I recall, initially four of them. The first one was in Obudovac, the second in Kruskovo Polje, the third in Pelagicevo, the fourth in Bosanski Samac. And that was the one that was most prominently Yugoslav by its composition because roughly one-third of the detachment was composed of members of other ethnicities.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the 1st Detachment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'd like to just note for the record I found this 65 ter summary to be very difficult to understand and difficult to prepare on. And I'd like note that for the past ten pages -- I think now we are getting into an area which seems to fall into the 65 ter summary, but for the past ten page there was literally no notice other than in May 1991 the witness left Zagreb and served as a JNA reserve officer in the Brcko garrison. We had absolutely no information about anything that's been led in the past ten pages. I'd like to just put that on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, any response to that or would you agree with Ms. Marcus?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with all due respect, I disagree. The summary stated that the witness would speak to the events in Bosanski Samac in the run-up to the takeover, as well as about all the other events at around this time. And all these issues we have been discussing in the past couple of pages were the circumstances surrounding the takeover of power of Samac in 1992, and this is merely an introduction into these events. That's how I see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the position of both parties is hereby on the record. Please proceed, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, sir, you mentioned the 1st Detachment. Can you tell us what was the area of responsibility of the 1st Detachment?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: Obudovac, Batkusa, and some other small hamlets. There would be a great many if I were to list them here. And they ran along a stretch that had on its opposite side the Croatian forces that had already been equipped an armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know who Andjelko Maslic is?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: I know the gentleman very well, Andjelko Maslic. He was the deputy president of the Presidency of the SFRY, and intellectual who hailed from Bosanski Samac who helped right the books entitled ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you just tell us if you know him and, if so, what was the position he occupied in the period we're discussing.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: I know him back from the time when I was -- when he was the secretary of the Presidency of the SFRY. As Yugoslavia broke up, he was retired and he hails from Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djukic. Do you know if Mr. Maslic helped establish contacts with certain military structures in this period of time?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: Of course he did. He was in touch with a pensioned general, Pekic, who hailed from Kordun in Croatia. Together with him he provided the necessary assistance and advice, insisting with the competent institutions that the Serbian people in Posavina be protected.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, do you know who Blagoje Simic is; and if so what is the position that the person occupied in early 1992?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: I know Blagoje Simic from before. I met with him repeatedly in 1991. He was the president of the Serbian Democratic Party. He was the chairman of the Bosanski Samac regional board, as well as for the board of Doboj. This is something that you didn't ask me about. Because I joined the multi-ethnic social democrats, I had many problems that I experienced from the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djukic, do you know in the spring of 1992, what was the relationship between Blagoje Simic and the leadership of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: He was one of the most trusted men among -- for the president of the SDS, Mr. Radoslav Karadzic -- Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us in a sentence what was the security situation like in 1992 in Posavina?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: Catastrophic, in a word. And I could use up another hundred to describe what it was like.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us exactly where the village of Sijekovac is located; and did something important happen there in the spring of 1992?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: I think it was the 23rd of March that the regular Croatian forces entered Sijekovac collecting crimes on a mass scale. Several days later they captured Derventa.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You say that they were Croatian forces. Where did they come from; if you know?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: Well, I did say earlier on that the Sava divides Slavonski Brod and Bosanski Brod. They came from the direction of Bosanski Brod, and I don't know which parts of Croatia these forces had originally come from. I don't have that sort of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, what was the situation like in Bosanski Samac proper, in the spring of 1992?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: Bosanski Samac was inhabited by representatives of three ethnicities. The president of the executive committee was one Jovanovic. The vice-president was Izet Izetbegovic. And the coalition of the Muslims and Croats was the dominant one. Otherwise, demographically, the Muslims were the most numerous in the area, and the Serbs were next.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djukic, was there a staff established of the Muslim forces or the Muslim people in Bosanski Samac in the spring of 1992?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: On the 12th or the 13th of April, Alija Izetbegovic established a TO War Staff that was composed solely of the Muslims and Croats. There wasn't a single Serb in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you repeat the date, please. It's not recorded properly.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: It was the 12th or the 13th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think this is the time for our first break today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will take a break. And we resume at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I apologise for the late start. There was an urgent matter which needed my attention which prevented me from returning in time. Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djukic, before the break you mentioned the TO staff, the war TO staff, that was -- that comprised Croats and Muslims alone. Could you tell us who was at the head of that war-time staff?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: I believe his name was Izet Fitozovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could the witness please be shown P221.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Now please take a look at the document before you on the screen, on the left-hand side.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: I was correct. But my apologies, his name was Alija, not Izet.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us if you recognise the individuals mentioned here as staff members? And could you tell us if you know anything about these people?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: Well, I do know these people. Sulejman Tihic and another person I know very well, but I would appreciate if we could move to private session for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we please move into private session previously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djukic, without mentioning any names, the names that you mentioned a moment ago, please tell us how you know that these individuals were involved in the trafficking -- illicit trafficking of weapons from Croatia into Bosnia and Herzegovina, the central part of Bosnia and Herzegovina. How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: Well, I have to explain first that I received certain tasks from the security and intelligence organ, the corps security and intelligence organ, and that I had a very high duty in the main security and intelligence organ in the Army of Republika Srpska. So some of the information comes from intercepts, some from direct knowledge, some from citizen complaints, to the effect that police officers would just observe how weapons were being transported by members of Croat or Muslim ethnicity onto trucks with Croatian or Slovene registration plates.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djukic. You mentioned the way that these -- this materiel was obtained. Now, can you tell us whether you know if any individuals were in charge of transferring materiel and technical equipment for the SDA and the war-time staff that you spoke about a little earlier?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: The village Prut and all the other villages - and I don't want to waste this Chamber's precious time - but all the villages between Samac and Orasje were Croatian, so there was no way of checking the transport of weapons by individuals across the Sava from Croatia into the Croatian villages in Bosnia where they established some military units and combat groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, you said that you knew about the existence of this war-time staff. Now, do you know whether any unit was established by the SDA in Bosanski Samac in the spring of 1992?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, sir, please tell us who was at the head of the public security station in Bosanski Samac in April 1992?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: It was Vinko Dragicevic. He was a representative of the Croatian side because this was a Muslim/Croat/Serb coalition at the time. Dragan Lukac was the chief of the crime police. Stoko Sekulic was the commander of the public security station, and they were there as representatives of the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, sir, what was the position of the Serbian Democratic Party in Bosanski Samac? What was their position on the work of the public security station in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: Well, the position of the SDS and the Serb population was the following. Irrespective of the composition and what ethnicity the members were, the public security station was not capable of protecting all the vital aspects and security of people and security of their property.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, sir, do you know whether the -- the SDA organised a citizen group that was supposed to defend the town of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: Well, it was only established later on when we came across some lists, a certain Atizovic or Elezovic went through Samac and the surrounding villages with the so-called Liljani, a small unit, which was called Liljani because it had the patch of the Muslim side -- of the Muslim party at the time which is now renamed into Bosnia party, and they were Lilies.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please have the witness shown 65 ter 3751 from the Prosecution list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, could I invite you again to give a good example to the witness how to make a pause between the one speaking person and the other speaking person.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will do my best, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, sir, this is a document that was produced by the TO Staff of Bosanski Samac. And I would like to refer you to -- this document is dated the 13th of April, 1992. Now I would like to show you the second page. Page 2. If you recall, we showed you this document during the proofing. This is a list of six pages containing the names of 212 individuals. Did you have occasion to see this document earlier; or, in other words, did we show you this document during proofing?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Judging by the names that appear on the list, could you tell us what ethnicity the individuals whose names appear on this list of self-organised citizens of Bosanski Samac are, the list that was compiled on the 13th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: Well, again, as I said, at the head of all of this was Sulejman Tihic. He was the leader. And we can see his name appearing on top -- on the top. And then following his name are Bosnian names, all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we would like to tender this document as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: No objection. Except it seems that the translation is missing a couple of pages. But, obviously, there's no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, part of the evidence is that all the names are Muslim names. And, under those circumstances, I think, Ms. Marcus, that to have the original names would be good enough, or do you insist on having them transcribed, I would say, rather than translated; although, there is, of course -- now and then there is some explanation, apparently units to which they belong or perhaps addresses. Until now, there's only about names. Do you insist on having it completed?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: If Your Honours are satisfied with that, I agree with that. Of course, the descriptions, as you say, Your Honour, are not translated but the names are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now. There is one other -- yes. That is, one name is -- is -- is -- are all the pages missing with names in translation? All of them are missing. Then, Mr. Petrovic, at least the title above the list of names should be translated. Therefore --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- there's no need to have all the names translated, or at least if no further evidence will be elicited on this matter. But at least the -- the title above the first name on the list should be translated, so we will mark it for identification. The original is then many, many pages, and the English will then be two pages when you have completed that job. Mr. Registrar, the number would be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter document 3751 shall be assigned Exhibit D762, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And keeps that status until [Overlapping speakers]...

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We will do as ordered by you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, we spoke of the public security station in Bosanski Samac and its activities. You told us what the position of the SDS was in respect of that station in April of 1992. Was it the case that the SDS took a decision of some sort in April of 1992 with regard to the running of the Samac public -- public security station?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: Let me just add that it wasn't just the SDS that was dissatisfied with their work. It was the citizens themselves as well. It was decided that a more efficient and improved service should be set up, both in terms of operations and the provision of services.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, did you participate in a meeting which discussed the ways and means of organising the work of the Samac public security station?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: I did say that I did not enjoy credibility with the SDS. It was through Petar Stevic and Lazo Mrkic, both of whom were friends of mine, and Stevic was also a member of the service, we were told that in the building of Agroposavina on the 12th of April, I should help build up an organisation equipped with all the required materiel and assets that a public security station should have.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djukic, can you tell us who referred you to that meeting?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: Nobody did. I went to that meeting as a person who was familiar with the way a public security station should be organised and run. Admittedly, I did tell Commander Nikolic that I would attend the meeting. He told me, I will not interfere with the business of the police and the civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you learnt that certain volunteers had arrived in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, it was at this very meeting that I learnt it. Stevan Todorovic, also known as Steve, and I would style him the monstrum, or the monster. We heard that he had 20 man who landed in the village of Batkusa by helicopter in the area of responsibility of the 1st Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whose helicopter it was that these people disembarked from in the village of Batkusa?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: I can't. Had I seen the helicopter, I would have been able to tell you. I can only tell you that that sort of helicopter that could carry as men was in the possession of only the JNA. I think it was the Knin Corps which, at the time, was still headed by General - perhaps Colonel - Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you learn under whose command it was that this group of volunteers came, if they came under any command upon their arrival in Batkusa?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: The arrival of this group of volunteers did cause some discomfort to the town itself, an uneasiness and reservation on the part of the inhabitants because Obudovac, Donji Zabari, and Pelagicevo had many capable trained young money who had done their military service. Therefore, Commander Stevan Nikolic was asked to account for the presence of these volunteers and to say who it was who needed them in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, did Stevan Nikolic give any sort of explanation and did you learn under whose command they were?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: Stevan Nikolic asked to be given a day or two until such time as his officers would get in touch with them in person to find out who they were and who they would be working for, if they were there to chase individuals away from the area, or to protect the area, or something quite different.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Two or three days later, what was the conclusion that the officers of Stevan Nikolic arrived at?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: Well, these individuals, conscripts, volunteers - what should I call them? - all agreed that they would voluntarily join the JNA and be resubordinated to the detachments under the 17th Tactical Group. They also agreed that they would perform the tasks given conscientiously. Some joined the 1st Detachment, others the 2nd, depending on their personal abilities, earlier experience, and skills.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djukic, who it was who took over the public security station in Samac, and when?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: But of course. That was the day of the Bosanski Samac municipality. In the night between the 16th and the 17th of April, it was Todorovic who took over; Stevo Todorovic, also known as Steve. He organised matters the way that I had envisaged, at least in terms of numbers. Stevic was the one who made the organigram, and he said that all those who accepted the SDS would be on the police force. He even said that, in that case, I would not be allowed on because I did not support the SDS. But I wasn't interested in that to begin with.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, sir, what sort of steps did Colonel Nikolic take that night between the 16th and the 17th of April?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: Well, there were different accounts, including those from the JNA, as to what was happening in the station that night. In my personal view, based on my experience, it was a tactical measure, an extensive raid with a view to seizing weapons from citizens who had great amounts of both military and hunting weapons in their possession. Colonel Nikolic was not kept abreast of these things. However, when he got word of it on the morning of the 17th, he called into -- in -- into the centre two armoured vehicles to come in as a show of force. He ordered the command of the detachment that they should come out to the Bosna river-bank right away since the Croatian village of Prut was already organised, under arms, and did not recognise the authorities in Samac. They were linked in terms of organisation and territory to the municipality of Odzak. On the other hand, the partially damaged bridge across the Sava allowed the Croats to carry out an incursion into Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, can we look at D18, please. Witness, this is a report sent to the General Staff of the SFRY armed forces on the 17th of April. It was sent out from the command of the 2nd Military District. It is a report relating to the events in Samac. In the middle of the page it reads: "The activities with a view to seizing the vital institutions, they were carried out with the participation of the forces of the Tactical Group 17, units of the Serbian Territorial Defence, and the police." Can you tell us what sort of the police force is referred to here?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: Well, the active police force of the public security station in Bosanski Samac. Quite understandably, there was the participation of the 17th Tactical Group as well because there was a detachment of 55 men within it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. You mentioned the 4th Detachment, which included Simo Zaric, among others. Do you know if there were members of other ethnicities in that detachment, in addition to the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: In the leadership of the staff itself, there were two Muslims and one Croat. There were the brothers Topcagic and one Vukovic. Now the unit, there were admittedly only a handful of Croats but there were around 100 Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, do you know these individuals who were members of the 4th Detachment? How were they characterised by the War Staff of the SDA and the SDA itself in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: They were labelled as national traitors. They were suspected of preparing an attack on Bosanski Samac. I'm sorry if I have to expand on this, but we had a number of intercepts, and we received information from General Kukanjac to the effect that occupation was being prepared, and Kukanjac said that this was the only useful and helpful thing he did in his life. Now, for these individuals, they were called either ethnic or national traitors; something to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Please look at P219. It is a proclamation entitled: "The List of Local Traitors" or "Domestic Traitors." The first one on the list is Fadil Topcagic. Do you know him?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. He was one of the finest explosive specialists. And --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness please repeat the last part of his answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was one of the leaders of the detachment, an assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you -- part of your last answer was not understood by the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Something was ordered but then it --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: -- it was given up on as an idea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please resume. You said when asked about Fadil: "Yes, of course. He was one of the finest explosive specialists and ..." Could you repeat what you then said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Later on, we were in a position to work on a mission together but the command decided that we should abort the mission. I had high regard for him as an excellent officer, and I said that he was Commander Antic's assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May Mr. Stanisic be excused for the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And we continue meanwhile. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you mentioned an intercept involving Kukanjac. What were the contents of the intercept and how did you come by it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: It was a dispatch, a document that I didn't receive. It was encoded and then decoded in the command of Commander Nikolic, and he shared this information with his officers, including myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you kindly tell us what the dispatch said, the one that Nikolic told you about and that he had received from General Kukanjac?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: There was severe criticism there, that there was poor -- that the defence of Samac was poorly organised, that the Croatian forces were preparing themselves, and that we should expect them to seize the area and commit massacre against the people. And he judged that the 17th Tactical Group was incapable of the job, of doing the job.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you said that the volunteers who had arrived Batkusa placed themselves under the command of the 1st Detachment and in parts of the 2nd Detachment of the 17th Tactical Group. Do you know if at some point an attack was planned and carried out against Modrica?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: It was the 17th Tactical Group that mounted an attack on Modrica. As an officer for intelligence and security, I was not duty-bound to participate in combat, nor did I want to. There was an order to that effect, the area was successfully captured, and the tactical group moved into this ethnically mixed town of Modrica as well as into certain villages. I don't know who ordered - it was the superior command, at any rate - that the units of the tactical group should withdraw so that the Serbian forces had to recapture the area, that's to say, Modrica, again. And as the tactical group first moved in, it didn't come across any significant resistance.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can Mr. Petrovic please repeat the number of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the number of the document, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies. P1413.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, have a look at the first paragraph, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness be shown page 1 of the document, please. Thank you. Can the witness look at the first paragraph of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, based on the localities mentioned here - if you know them, of course - if this has to do with the first or some other attack on Modrica? And look at the date. It's the 7th of May, 1992. Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this please be enlarged for the witness so that he can read the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you want me to read it for you?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: This is a document from the command of the 17th Tactical Group dated the 7th of May, 1992, in Pelagicevo, to Lugar command. An order for an attack. And it says: "I have decided ..." Under 1: "In order to create favourable conditions for Modrica units, to enable them to continue their combat and capture the town of Modrica, link up with the units of the 17th Tactical Group that had been cut off in the area of the villages of Donji Skugric and Tolisa, carry out an all-out attack along the axis of Milosevac village-Garevac village-Modrica and Kornica village-Cardak village-Pustara, agricultural combine -- or agricultural co-operative." Could you tell us which Modrica attack does this refer to? You mentioned some.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: Well, obviously this is the first attack on Modrica. Stevan Nikolic, on orders from the General Staff, left Posavina on 19th of May. Therefore, the second attack and the takeover of Modrica was carried out by the newly established units of the VRS after his withdrawal from Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: After the JNA withdrew from Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, under number 2 we see that there are tasks assigned to the units and it says that the north column composed of the Lugar Group; the central column, under 2, Column Commander Captain Grbic; and under 3, the southern column --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which, Your Honours, is on the next page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: The column commander is Crni. Now, looking at this, do you know -- these columns that are mentioned in this order, what -- which group did they belong to?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: Well, they were part of the 17th Tactical Group, but I can't tell you exactly by platoon or detachment who belonged to what or where. But I can just tell that you these are volunteers, Lugar and Djordjevic, whereas in the central part, that person there is an active-duty officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When you say in the central part, whom are you referring to? Do you mean the second column?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness, sir. Witness, sir, you mentioned that at the meeting in Agroposavina, you learned of the arrival of these volunteers. Can you tell us, do you know whether there was any clash between Simo Zaric and Colonel Nikolic because of these volunteers who had arrived in Batkusa area?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't really accept that. You can't say that there can be a conflict between a colonel and a sergeant. There can be a dialogue, a lot polemics. Simo considered the volunteers would --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not understand the witness.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: -- members of the platoon who are not Serbs. Although there were other reasons too, Simo was very ambitious and he would probably be satisfied --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could I ask you -- first of all, again, that you would slow down. But to resume your previous answer, you said. "Well, I couldn't really accept that. You can't say there could be a conflict between a colonel and ..." Could you resume your answer from there, because the interpreters could not understand you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise yet again. There were debates and there was protest by Simo Zaric. He told Nikolic that Posavina had a sufficient number of young, brave, and capable men, that they did not need volunteers because members of his detachment who were Muslims or Croats would leave the detachment and the detachment would no longer be multi-ethnic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, sir, could you tell us what Nikolic replied when he complained in this manner?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: Well, Nikolic said that on the 28th of February, Croatian paramilitary units crossed over into Bosanski Brod, that the Croatian villages were full of combat groups, that there was some person there who was bringing in Liljani into Bosanski Samac, that he was disturbed by 20 Serbs from Serbia, that the government of Serbia, in a decree of 1992, proclaimed that volunteers could report to fight.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, could you tell us whether at some point you met a person called Srecko Radovanovic, aka Debeli?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I met that person. A Chetnik duke.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us where you met him and under what circumstances?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: I met him in Obudovac village, where my mother came from, and I had a friend there, Niko Bojic, who sold petrol products. He told me, he bragged that a very capable officer had come, and he took me to a room which was the headquarters of the 1st Battalion. I was introduced to that person. He showed [realtime transcript read in error "told"] me a Chetnik booklet number 2. He asked me whether I knew who had -- who was the owner of the Chetnik booklet number 1, and I said I didn't, and it wasn't my flavour, as it were, that these people had been conquered, and if we do have to fight, then we should keep the profile of Serb officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did he tell you who was the bearer of that Chetnik booklet, booklet number 1?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: Certainly. He said it was Duke Seselj. And in view of my position and my ideology and everything I knew from 1978 and onwards, he was one of the leading enemies of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may, on page 48, line 16 of the transcript, it says, "He told me," and I believe it should read, "He showed me."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, well, Mr. Petrovic, as always we do not fill in what it should be but we could verify whether "he told me" is right. You told us about Niko Bojic who sold petrol products. And then what did you then say? It now reads: "He told me, I bragged that a very capable officer had come and he took me to a room which was the headquarters of the 1st Battalion." The part which reads, "He told me," is that accurate or is that a mistake?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me just clarify it. Yes, he had a petrol station. He was the owner of a petrol station. He did not deal in petrol products illegally. He was an acquaintance and he worked in Zupanja.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was not asking you to further explain to us but just whether the words which we find on our transcript, "He told me," whether that's perhaps wrong and should be something else.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. He told me that a very capable officer had arrived in Obudovac and that he wanted to introduce me to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please. I had a wrong line, as a matter of fact, where I sought the clarification. Did he tell you about the Chetnik booklet number 2 or did he show that to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He showed it to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Petrovic, I made a mistake. You referred me to line 16, whereas I started reading at line 13 where the words "he told me" also appear, but I didn't listen well enough to you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, sir, in addition to this one meeting at your friend's place in Obudovac, did you have any other occasion to talk to Srecko Radovanovic aka Debeli?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us when and in what circumstances?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: After Colonel Nikolic left the area, because my elder son had been injured, my younger son was still there, and my wife was a refugee, I myself tried to leave Posavina. In the meantime, the new commander of the Tactical Group - at that time already a brigade - was appointed, Lieutenant-Colonel Djordjevic, who was a local man, and his successor Dragan Djordjevic, Crni; whereas, Srecko was appointed chief. I told him how threatened my village was. It was -- we were expecting to be attacked, and the structure of our fighting force was very bad. There were men between 70 -- to 70 years old. I asked him to provide some reinforcement and I proposed an operation, that we should try and cut off a -- an operation -- or, rather, an action by the Croatian side --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to repeat the last portion of his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you repeat the last portion of your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To cut off the communication between the Bosanska, Bijelo, and Dubrava villages, the road, which was used by forces that intended to take up positions, Croatian and Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, the meeting you had with Radovanovic, do you remember what was said? What did he say? What did you say to him? Can you recall thank conversation?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can. I can recall the conversation. He said that they had to fight really hard to be appointed to those duties, that they were the first people - members of the brigade - who had not graduated from the Military Academy of the Yugoslav army. He told me that it was a great pity that I was on the wrong side, that I was not a member of the SDS. And only after I explained to him who I was and that I had passed with my units without any losses, he told me that he had been a police non-commissioned officer, that he was dismissed from the police, that he had a very negative view of us, people who still supported Tito's ideology, Milosevic's ideology, and that of the Communist party of Yugoslavia. And he asked me once again to try and change my position. And he even said that if I were to join this radical party that I might even be conferred a rank there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, line -- page 51, line 16, a party is mentioned there which is -- which was incorrectly interpreted. So I propose that we ask the witness to clarify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, sir, Radovanovic told you that you took the wrong side, that you weren't a member of what party?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: The Serbian Radical Party, which had a Chetnik wing, a military arm, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. During these encounters of yours, did Srecko Radovanovic, Debeli, mention that he had certain links with the state security service of the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: Quite the contrary. He said that he was abhorred by the likes of me and others who refused to accept the ideas promoted by Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, sir, you mentioned an individual by the name of Crni, Dragoljub Djordjevic, Crni. Can you tell us did you have occasion to meet with him?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DJUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I knew of him as Dragan. This is the first time I hear of him as Dragoljub. If that is the individual from Vranje, the same Crni, then that is him.
